newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Zhivkov-last living communist strongman.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Zhivkov-last living communist strongman.

text.p: Former Bulgarian president Todor Zhivkov, released from house arrest on Monday at the height of political and economic protests, was eastern Europe's longest serving leader until his removal in a bloodless coup in 1989.
Sofia prosecutor Mikhail Doichev said he had ordered the release of the former communist dictator following a decision from the chief prosecutor's office.

"He is an old man, and in view of his health he should be free to move round town," Doichev said. He said Zhivkov had to inform the prosecutor's office if he wanted to leave Sofia or change his residence.
Zhivkov was convicted in 1992 of embezzling 21.5 million levs (then about $24 million) of public funds for luxury apartments and Western cars for his family and favoured aides.
Last February the Supreme Court overturned the sentence but he still needed permission to leave his granddaughter's villa in Sofia's wealthy Boyana suburb.
Zhivkov, now 85, ruled Bulgaria for 35 years until the collapse of his hardline communist regime in 1989.
A one-time associate of late Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev and Romania's Nicolae Ceausescu, he is one of Eastern Europe's last surviving communist leaders.

Despite allegations of corruption, he remained popular with many Bulgarians nostalgic for the simpler days of one-party rule when the state ensured cheap bread while hindering freedom of speech and movement.
Zhivkov was ousted by the Communist Party Central Committee in November 1989 and replaced by his foreign minister, the more reform-minded Petar Mladenov.
Diplomats said his refusal to loosen Bulgaria's centralised economy had been largely responsible for his downfall.
Although he publicly embraced the reform policies of Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, he maintained a firm grip on power, removing potential reformers from positions of authority.
In his decades as party leader, Zhivkov strove to mould Bulgaria into Moscow's staunchest ally.
Signs of strain emerged after the 1982 death of Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev and persisted into Gorbachev's tenure in the Kremlin.

Bulgaria's international image also suffered from U.S. charges that Bulgaria was involved in drug-trafficking, as well as allegations that its intelligence services were implicated in an attempt on the life of Pope John Paul II.

The Bulgarian economy, once one of the steadiest in East Europe, ran into trouble in the mid-1980s when successive droughts ruined its main crops and harsh winters hit the energy sector at a time when the Soviet Union was cutting oil exports.

Ham-fisted central planning by Zhivkov's regime reduced the national economy to chaos, leaving his successors with a $10 billion foreign debt and stagnant state industries propped up by lavish subsidies.
Less flamboyant than neighbouring Ceausescu, Zhivkov gained a reputation for petty vanity and for lavishing luxuries on family and associates.

His daughter Lyudmilla, who died in 1981, was minister of culture. His son Vladimir held a number of senior political posts, and grandson Todor Slavkov was sent to an expensive Swiss university, allegedly at state expense. Slavkov is on bail, accused of rape.
A keen hunter, Zhivkov collected official residences, hunting lodges, a luxury yacht and a private train, all of which were confiscated after his fall from power.
Todor Zhivkov was born on September 7, 1911, in the Balkan mountain village of Pravets outside Sofia. After an elementary education he worked in a Sofia printing firm.
Following a spell in the Communist Youth League, he joined the Communist Party in 1932, holding district-level posts in the party's hierarchy until the start of World War Two.

During the German occupation he organised partisans in the Sofia area and helped in the Communist takeover on September 9, 1944. After the war he rose to become a full member of the ruling party politburo with a power base in Sofia.
In 1971, with virtually all his rivals neutralised, he moved from premier to become head of state as well as party chief.
He was married but became a widower in 1971. His granddaughter is a succesful fashion designer.
